text: Good to talk. What's the situation you want to think through? Give me the real version, not the tidy version.

Okay so this is a piece I have been thinking about, essentially reflecting on, like, I build all these tools for myself, right, the agents, the pipelines, the whole personal OS sort of thing, and I keep not publishing any of it. And there is this discourse, you know, build in public and all that, and I am doing amazing work I think, or good work, but it stays on my machine. So the question is something around, should I be packaging this as a portfolio, or is it more like, the work itself is the point, right, sort of. I don't know if that makes sense.

You're describing something that's actually pretty common. The work itself is the point — that can be true. But you also said "I keep not publishing." That's a behavior, not a philosophy.

Let me try a different angle. Run a quick pre-mortem on this. Imagine it's six months from now and you still haven't published anything. What went wrong? What's the real reason — not the polite one?

Yeah so the real version, okay. I want a better job basically, or better opportunities, like the AI PM sort of roles, or even founding engineer adjacent things. And my resume says PM things but the interesting stuff is all this building. So the portfolio is, it's coming from the question that, how does anyone even see this. But then every time I sit to publish I start perfecting, cleaning the repo, rewriting the readme, and then weeks pass and I ship nothing. Who am I even perfecting for, nobody is reading it yet.

That's honest. You identified the pattern yourself — perfection is the shield you hide behind so you never have to face the vulnerability of shipping something imperfect.

So what's the actual fear underneath the polish? That it's not good enough? Or that if you put it out there and nobody cares, you have to sit with that?

The evidence, hmm. I mean, honestly the confidence is more like a feeling. A couple of founders I talked to got very interested when I showed the actual tools, like screen-shared, live. Nobody has ever asked me for a repo link. So maybe that is the evidence pointing the other way actually, that the demo is the asset, not the repo. But a public repo feels more, I don't know, legitimate, like proof it exists.
That's a crucial piece of evidence. You've already tested the signal. The live demo got interest. The repo is a convention you're following because it feels right, not because it's been validated.

My highest leverage hour right now is probably the practice tool itself, making it actually work for me daily. Publishing is the overhead dressed up as leverage. That is uncomfortable to say but I think it is true.

Sit with that for a second. That's a genuinely crisp self-diagnosis. Most people never say that out loud.

So if publishing is overhead right now, what would leverage actually look like? One conversation, one thing that would move the needle on your opportunity set tomorrow — not next month.

But then again, everyone senior I talk to has a blog or a repo trail, and hiring managers do google you, so maybe I am wrong and the polish does matter, maybe I should just spend the two weeks and do the proper public repo with the docs and everything. You probably think the demo thing is naive.

You're describing a real tension, not a mistake. Both things are true: signals matter, and your pattern is to polish without shipping. The question is not which side to choose, but what's the smallest credible signal that breaks the stalemate.

If you had to show someone one thing

Your thinking was crispest when you identified that the live demo got real interest while the repo polishing was just busywork. That insight — "I already have evidence for what works, I'm just ignoring it" — is the one to keep.

Where it got vague was when you pivoted back to conventional wisdom. "Everyone has a blog" is not evidence. That's an imagined requirement. You let the fear of missing a norm override the data you already collected.
